task.name: Stale-worktree sweep deletes never-pushed story branches, destroying committed work
task.story_text:
## Observed behavior

The stale-worktree sweep deletes a story worktree whose branch has never been
pushed, destroying committed work that is not present anywhere else. A branch
that has not yet been published is indistinguishable, to this check, from one
that was deleted after merging.

In sprint `a865b3e0fe03` (2026-07-27), story #1945 was actively running — the
sprint had it at `REVIEW cycle=2`, 50 minutes elapsed — with two commits in its
worktree and a clean working tree. A mid-run re-exec re-entered sprint startup,
and the sweep removed it:

```
[forge] DROPPED issue-1945: active worktree collision after re-exec; continuing with remaining stories.
[forge] 08:37:50.474 ⚠ WORKSPACE  stale worktree detected — removing feat/issue-1945
[forge] 08:37:50.474   sweep: merged or branch gone
[forge] 08:37:51.947   Removed stale worktree: /Users/pwickersham/src/theforge/.forge/worktrees/issue-1945
```

The branch was neither merged nor gone. It held `ac61b39` and `c3aed46` —
800 insertions across 13 files, including four new test modules — none of it
pushed, because the story had not yet reached a pull request. The commits
survived only as unreachable objects and were recovered by hand from
`git fsck --lost-found`.

The same story had already lost a previous attempt's work the day before, so
this was the second destruction of the same story's output.

## Diagnosis

**Observed symptom:** a running story's worktree was deleted as stale, and its
committed work was reachable afterwards only through the object store.

**Evidence — the staleness predicate asks the remote.**
`src/theforge/coordinator/workspace.py:604` determines whether a branch is gone
by looking for a remote-tracking ref:

```python
ok_gone, gone_out = _cu._run_shell(
    f"git rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/remotes/origin/{branch_name}", project_root
)
branch_gone = not ok_gone or not gone_out.strip()
```

A story branch created locally and not yet pushed has no
`refs/remotes/origin/<branch>`, so `branch_gone` is true for every story that
has not yet opened a pull request. The removal at `:619` then fires under the
message "merged or branch gone", which is accurate for the merged case and
false for this one.

**Evidence — the safety check does not cover committed work.** Immediately
before, `:601` skips any worktree with a dirty tree:

```python
ok_status, status_out = _cu._run_shell("git status --porcelain", candidate)
if not ok_status or status_out.strip():
    continue
```

The guard protects *uncommitted* changes. Work that a dev agent has committed
leaves a clean tree, so a story that is doing exactly what it is supposed to do
— committing as it goes — passes the guard and is eligible for deletion. The
better the agent's commit hygiene, the more it stands to lose.

**Evidence — the story was live.** The sprint's own status showed #1945 at
`REVIEW cycle=2` with 50 minutes elapsed and `$8.19` recorded when the sweep
ran, and an agent process group belonging to that worktree was still alive
afterwards, later reaped as orphaned.

**Ruled out — the sweep being wrong to exist.** Reclaiming worktrees whose
branches have merged is legitimate housekeeping. The defect is the predicate,
not the cleanup.

**Ruled out — this being specific to re-exec.** The re-exec is what caused the
sweep to run while a story was mid-flight, but the predicate is wrong
independently: any sweep encountering an unpushed story branch with a clean tree
will remove it. The re-exec determines the timing, not the outcome.

**Confirmed cause:** absence of a remote-tracking ref is used as evidence that a
branch has been deleted, when it equally denotes a branch that has not yet been
published. Deletion of local-only history is gated on a condition that local-only
history satisfies by definition.

**Fix-success criterion:** a worktree whose branch holds commits absent from the
remote is never removed by the sweep, and a branch that has never been pushed is
distinguished from one whose remote ref was deleted after merging. Given #1945
as input, the sweep leaves the worktree in place and the two commits remain
reachable.

## Expected behavior

Automated cleanup must not be able to destroy the only copy of something. The
question a reclamation step has to answer is whether the work it is about to
discard exists somewhere else, and a check that reads as "has this been
integrated" has to actually establish integration rather than infer it from a
signal that unfinished work also produces. Where the two cannot be told apart,
the safe reading is the one that preserves.

This is sharper for work a system produced on the operator's behalf. Commits
created by an agent inside a worktree have no other home until they are pushed,
so the window in which they exist only locally is not an edge case but the
normal condition of every story before it opens a pull request. A cleanup pass
that treats that window as evidence of abandonment is at odds with the workflow
that creates it.

Finally, a guard that protects uncommitted changes but not committed ones
inverts the durability the operator expects. Committing is the act that is
supposed to make work safe, and a policy under which committed work is eligible
for deletion while a dirty tree is protected penalises exactly the behavior the
system asks its agents to perform.

handoff.summary: sweep_orphan_worktrees no longer infers branch deletion from the absence of refs/remotes/origin/<branch>. A new helper _count_unpublished_commits() runs `git rev-list --count <branch> --not --remotes=origin` to count commits that no origin remote-tracking ref contains; the sweep skips (and logs) any candidate with a non-zero count, and also skips when the count cannot be determined (command failure or unparseable output). The guard runs before the existing merged/branch_gone decision, so a branch whose commits are all reachable from origin is still reclaimed exactly as before, while a never-pushed branch holding committed work — the normal state of every story before it opens a PR — is preserved. The removal log line now names which case fired (merged into origin/base vs remote branch gone) and records that no commits were missing from origin. Four new tests cover: never-pushed branch with two commits preserved with history intact, published-merged-then-remote-ref-deleted branch still removed, unpublished branch with no commits of its own still removed, and undeterminable count preserving. One pre-existing test's setup was corrected (see story_deviations).

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A worktree whose branch holds commits absent from the remote is never removed by the sweep.
acceptance_criteria.notes: workspace.py:621 skips removal whenever _count_unpublished_commits() returns a non-zero count, and fails safe (skips) when it returns None. Covered by test_sweep_preserves_never_pushed_branch_with_committed_work and test_sweep_preserves_worktree_when_unpublished_count_is_undeterminable. Verified load-bearing: stubbing the helper to return 0 reproduces the original deletion.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A branch that has never been pushed is distinguished from one whose remote ref was deleted after merging.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Both cases lack refs/remotes/origin/<branch>; the unpublished-commit count separates them — never-pushed work yields >0 and is preserved, merged-then-deleted yields 0 and is reclaimed. Covered by test_sweep_removes_branch_whose_remote_ref_was_deleted_after_merging alongside the preserve test.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Given #1945 as input, the sweep leaves the worktree in place and the two commits remain reachable.
acceptance_criteria.notes: test_sweep_preserves_never_pushed_branch_with_committed_work reconstructs that shape (unpushed branch, clean tree, two commits) and asserts the worktree, the branch tip sha, and both commits survive the sweep.

story_deviations: Adjusted setup in the existing test test_sweep_orphan_worktrees_removes_forge_only_orphans_and_merged_but_preserves_escalated: it merged forge/merged into local main but left origin/main stale, so the 'merged' branch had commits present on no origin ref — indistinguishable from unpushed work and now correctly preserved. Added `git fetch origin main:refs/remotes/origin/main` after the merge so the fixture reflects a PR that actually landed on the remote, matching the adjacent ..._still_checked_out_elsewhere test. No assertions or test intent changed.
deferred_items: _is_stale_worktree() (workspace.py:490) uses `git log <local base>..<branch>` for its commits-ahead guard rather than the origin-reachability check. It already preserves branches with commits, so it does not exhibit this defect, and no AC covers it; left as-is.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules
Keep modules single-purpose; extract instead of growing monolith files
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
